synopsis: SAE J1939 is the heavy-machine network language used by ISO/TS 21815-2:2021 for collision-device intervention; the technical specification was published in July 2021 and confirmed in December 2024 [f12976, f15025, f15146]. Its interface supports slow-down, controlled-stop, emergency-stop and motion-inhibit requests, plus capability discovery and keep-alive, but is explicitly not plug-and-play [f5910, f12979, f12980]. Across chapters, this standardized interface is presented as an off-road anchor for brake requests, a precedent for reusing evidence across machine models, and a natural HIL test interface that a bench can emulate [f5579, f367, f538, f8661]. Validation must cover end-to-end integration latency, adequate machine-state recording with message-schema versions, and protection against spoofing, stale messages, bus faults and incompatible implementations; SIL cannot demonstrate unexpected CAN/J1939 timing behavior [f8198, f12982, f2936, f530]. The booklet nevertheless identifies an omission of J1939 cybersecurity and integrity from its eight brake-timing questions, and warns that interface or controller changes in 2027 without impact analysis may invalidate the pre-built simulator [f6607, f11028].

relations.note: Both identify the standardized intervention interface as a precedent for cross-model evidence reuse.
Glossary adds July 2021 publication timing to the December 2024 confirmation.
Both report publication in July 2021 and confirmation in 2024.
Both list stop commands, capability discovery and keep-alive.
Both explicitly state that the interface is not plug-and-play.
Both define slow, stop and motion-prevention commands; the latter specifies standstill.
Both anchor the brake request in the ISO/TS 21815-2 J1939 interface.
Both require end-to-end integration-latency validation when intervention uses J1939.
Both describe bench emulation of stop, slow-down and motion-inhibit commands.
Both recommend HIL as the natural setting for testing the intervention interface.
Both describe HIL injection using camera data, radar detections and recorded CAN/J1939 traffic.
Both include ISO/TS 21815-2 J1939 emulation in the lowest-cost tool chain.
Both identify SA TS ISO 21815.2:2023 as covering the J1939 interface.
Glossary adds DBC and message-schema version recording to machine-state logging.
Specific unsafe-command threats detail the interface's safety and security significance.
Required interface security coverage is omitted from the brake-timing questions.
SIL's inability to expose bus timing behavior supports using HIL.
